      PLAINTIFF'S CONSOLIDATED REPLY IN SUPPORT OF ECF NOS. 90 AND 93


        Plaintiff replies to Meta's opposition, ECF No. 101, to Plaintiffs Rule 72(a) objections to

 ECF No. 84 (ECF Nos. 89, 90, 91) and to Plaintiffs motion for targeted vacatur (ECF Nos. 93,

 94). Plaintiff seeks correction of the challenged rulings and determination of the remaining relief

 on the existing submissions.

 I.     ECF NO. 84 RESTS ON A LEGAL PREMISE RULE 26(d)(l) DOES NOT
        PERMIT.
        ECF No. 84 states that "the Court cannot issue an order concerning Plaintiffs Motions

 because discovery has not officially begun in this case." ECF No. 84 at 1-2. Rule 26( d)(l) bars

 discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference "except ... when authorized by these rules, by

 stipulation, or by court order." Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(l). ECF Nos. 15 and 54 asked for that order.

 ECF No. 84 identifies the absence of ordinary discovery and a Scheduling Order as preventing the

 requested authorization. Rule 26( d)(l) expressly permits authorization by court order. The



                                                  1

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF           Document 102        Filed 10/28/26      Page 2 of 10 PageID#
                                           1042



 objection is to the legal reason the order gives. A court abuses its discretion when it "relies on

 erroneous factual or legal premises." Wall v. Rasnick, 42 F.4th 214, 220 (4th Cir. 2022) (quotation

 omitted).

         Meta answers that the Magistrate Judge "expressly construed Plaintiffs 'Motions as

 requests for expedited discovery."' ECF No. 101 at 4. The label does not resolve the objection.

 The sentence after the label states the premise Plaintiff challenges. Describing the motions as

 requests for early discovery does not change the reason the order gives for declining to authorize

 them.

         Meta also incorporates its arguments from ECF No. 73: that the requests should await the

 dismissal motions and that the answers would not help Plaintiff. ECF No. 101 at 4. Those are

 alternative grounds, and ECF No. 91 at 5-7 answers them. The seven interrogatories ask where

 the two reports originated, what identifying information they contained, and whether they were

 connected to any account Plaintiff held. ECF Nos. 15-1, 54-1. Each permits one of three answers.

 None asks for the reports. NCMEC states that Plaintiff "does not have access to those reports."

 ECF No. 74 at 5. That statement describes the gap: Defendants hold the records and seek dismissal

 with prejudice on the ground that the letters' statements are true. ECF No. 91 at 5-6. Plaintiff

 requests the answers now because Defendants' motions place the content of those records at issue

 before any Scheduling Order will issue. The proposed pleading states its claims without the

 answers. ECF No. 91 at 6-7. Whether to authorize the questions and whether any answer may be

 considered on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion are separate questions. The Court should authorize the

 requests on the existing showing or restore them for determination under Rule 26(d)(l). ECF No.

 90 ,r 16(±)-(g).




                                                 2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF            Document 102         Filed 10/28/26      Page 3 of 10 PageID#

 II.    META DOES NOT RESOLVE THE PENDING COMPARISON AND DEADLINE
        OBJECTIONS OR ESTABLISH FUTILITY OF THE PROPOSED PLEADING.
        Plaintiff does not dispute the Court's authority to require a comparison document. ECF No.

 91 at 11. Plaintiff produced none through October 7. The objections did not stay ECF No. 64. Id. at

 13-14. The question is whether denial of ECF No. 59, with the filed proposed pleading and the

 existing merits briefing before the Court, was the appropriate consequence. ECF No. 64 issued on

 September 9 and set September 11 as the compliance date. ECF No. 64. Plaintiffs declaration

 states that actual notice of ECF No. 64 arrived at about 9:09 p.m. on September 11. ECF No. 68-

 1 ,r,r 8- 9. On September 13 Plaintiff requested relief from the expired deadline under Rule 6(b )( 1)

 (B) and a compliance period keyed to a ruling on the baseline. ECF No. 67 ,r 7. No comparison

 followed through October 7. ECF No. 84 at 2. NCMEC called the initial missed deadline

 "understandable." ECF No. 74 at 4. ECF No. 84 found "ample opportunity" to comply. ECF No.

 84 at 2. It did not separately address the requested deadline relief or the baseline objection when

 making that finding. Those circumstances bore on whether denial, rather than a defined compliance

 period, was the appropriate response. Meta's opposition does not address them.

        Meta's chronology states that "[r]ather than comply with this order, Plaintiff filed Rule

 72(a) objections." ECF No. 101 at 2. The deadline expired on September 11. The objections were

 submitted on September 13 . ECF No. 67 ,r 5. The weeks of nonproduction that followed are a

 separate period, during which the request for deadline relief remained pending.

        ECF No. 64 required comparison against the original Complaint, ECF No. 1. ECF No. 59

 would replace the First Amended Complaint, ECF No. 5. ECF No. 59 ,r 3. A comparison against

 ECF No. 1 combines changes already made in ECF No. 5 with the changes now proposed. That is

 the basis for the request to reconsider or clarify the baseline. ECF No. 67 ,r 7. Vogel denied

 amendment without prejudice and permitted a renewed motion with clean and marked copies.



                                                   3

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF             Document 102         Filed 10/28/26       Page 4 of 10 PageID#
                                             1044



 Vogel v. RMAC Trust Series 2016-CTT, No. 1:24-cv-2182, ECF No. 37 at 1-2 (E.D. Va. Apr. 11,

 2025).

          Meta states that ECF No. 84 does not expressly preclude another request to amend with a

 comparison. ECF No. 101 at 6. Restoring ECF No. 59 permits determination on the submissions

 already filed: the proposed pleading, ECF No. 59-1; the memorandum, ECF No. 60; and the

 oppositions, ECF Nos. 73, 74, and 83. ECF No. 90 ,-r 16(d)-(e).

          Meta's futility argument rests on ECF No. 83, which adopts the applicable arguments of

 NCMEC and Hall and separately challenges the relevance of Meta's August 13, 2026 filing in the

 376 Action. ECF No. 83 at 1, 3; ECF No. 101 at 5. The proposed pleading pleads the August filing

 as a subsequent fact bearing on Meta's knowledge and state of mind and states that it "is not an

 independent basis for liability." ECF No. 59-1 ,-i 276. Plaintiff does not offer the August filing as

 proof of the April agreement. ECF No. 91 at 22. The inference of agreement rests on the April

 sequence: NCMEC and Meta received the same materials, ,-i 127; each moved against the same

 discovery, ,-i 128; Hall issued two case-specific letters the next day, before formal service and

 before any ruling, ,-i,-i 130-135; the letters served the deterrent purpose alleged, ,-i,-i 174-180; and

 the acts alleged are the issuance and transmission of those letters, ,-i,-i 181-184. Plaintiff asks the

 Court to assess those allegations together under the pleading standard. Section S, ECF No. 59-1 ,-i,-i

 203-215, is separate. It pleads on personal knowledge the account names Plaintiff used, ,-i,-i 204-

 209, and pleads on information and belief what the reports contained and whom they identified,

 ,-i,-i 211-214. Those allegations bear on falsity and on the Hall and NCMEC grounds answered at

 ECF No. 91 at 19-22. They do not themselves establish Meta's participation in an agreement.

 Futility should be assessed against the complete proposed pleading and the grounds already

 briefed.




                                                    4

                                            1045



 III.    REASSIGNMENT DOES NOT RESOLVE THE PENDING OBJECTIONS OR
         THE REQUESTED RETROSPECTIVE RELIEF.
         Meta argues that Rule 72(a) review "ensure[s]" that any errors "can be remedied through

 that review, rather than by vacating the orders." ECF No. 101 at 7. Meta identifies review that

 remains to be performed. Plaintiff requests that review and a determination of the remaining

 retrospective relief. Rule 72(a) directs the District Judge to consider timely objections and to

 "modify or set aside any part of the order that is clearly erroneous or is contrary to law." Fed. R.

 Civ. P. 72(a). The objections identify a legal premise (Part I), a finding made without addressing

 a pending request and a baseline objection (Part II), and the choice of denial as the consequence.

 Meta's reliance on available review does not establish what that review will resolve. Plaintiff has

 also requested independent determination of the restored motions. ECF No. 93 ,r 10(R4).

         Meta's authorities involved review already completed. In Brock the Second Circuit

 reviewed the dismissal "anew, without any deference" and had "already concluded that the district

 court did not err"; the second and third Liljeberg factors "weigh in favor of vacatur," and the first

 outweighed them. Brock v. Zuckerberg, No. 21-1796-cv, slip op. at 11-12 (2d Cir. Apr. 27, 2022)

 (summary order). In ExxonMobil "an unconflicted district judge then gave the case a fresh look-

 that is, she reviewed his decision de novo" on "pure questions of law." ExxonMobil Oil Corp. v.

 TIG Ins. Co., 44 F.4th 163, 174 (2d Cir. 2022). That procedure is the independent determination

 Plaintiff requests.

         Meta states that "there has been no finding of any violation of 28 U.S.C. § 455." ECF No.

 101 at 5. ECF No. 96 denied the disqualification motion as moot because "[t]he case has been

 reassigned." ECF No. 96. It did not decide whether Judge Davis held a qualifying interest on the

 dates of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, how any interest was held, whether knowledge existed where the

 statute requires it, or whether an exception applies. The annual reports document past holdings.



                                                  5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF              Document 102          Filed 10/28/26       Page 6 of 10 PageID#
                                              1046



 They are not a finding of qualifying ownership during the challenged rulings. ECF No. 93 ,-i 5.

 Plaintiff requests those findings to the extent necessary to determine the remaining statutory and

 retrospective relief, on the conditional terms stated in ECF No. 93 ,-i,-i 5 and 10(R2).

         Meta's remaining cases tum on their facts. In Chesher the entities whose stock the judge

 held had been voluntarily dismissed before the challenged rulings, and those rulings neither

 benefited nor bound them. Chesher v. 3M Co., No. 3:15-cv-2123-RMG, ECF No. 330 at 4-6

 (D.S.C. Jan. 6, 2022). Meta remains a party, and ECF No. 84 denied discovery directed to Meta.

 ECF No. 84 at 1. Litovich rejected later appellate review as an adequate answer in the

 circumstances of the documented conflict and the substantive proceedings before it. Litovich v.

 Bank ofAm. Corp., No. 21-2905, slip op. at 19-20 (2d Cir. July 2, 2024). Vacatur under§ 455 is

 neither categorical nor foreclosed; it turns on the risk of injustice to the parties, the risk of injustice

 in other cases, and the risk of undermining public confidence. Liljeberg v. Health Servs.

 Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 862-64 (1988).

         Those considerations apply on a short record. ECF No. 84 excluded the proposed pleading

 and denied the specified discovery. Three dismissal motions will otherwise be decided against a

 pleading Plaintiff moved to replace on September 7. ECF No. 94 at 5-6. Later discovery depends

 on the case continuing. If a qualifying conflict is established, the consequences of prior

 participation in those rulings require a determination. The requested procedure preserves every

 existing submission and requires no retrial. ECF No. 93 ,-i 10(R3).

 IV.     RELIEF
         Plaintiff requests that the Court: (1) set aside the challenged rulings in ECF No. 84; (2)

 remove the comparison prerequisite and vacate the September 11, 2026 deadline in ECF No. 64,

 determining the preserved objections in ECF Nos. 66 and 67 together with ECF No. 90; (3) grant

 ECF No. 59, deem ECF No. 59-1 the operative pleading, and authorize ECF Nos. 15 and 54 on the


                                                     6

                                           1047



 terms already requested; (4) alternatively, restore ECF Nos. 15, 54, and 59 for independent

 determination on their existing authorized submissions without an additional comparison; (5) if

 the Court sustains a comparison requirement, identify the baseline and set the compliance period

 requested in ECF No. 67 1 7; (6) determine ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76, including the request

 concerning ECF No. 76-1, on the coordinated basis stated in ECF No.901115-16; (7) determine

 the remaining statutory and retrospective relief under ECF No. 93 1 10 to the extent necessary,

 with any conflict-based vacatur matched to the established period and the particular orders; and

 (8) determine these matters before, or expressly within, any disposition ofECF Nos. 10, 21, or 45

 that would terminate a claim in reliance on the exclusion of ECF No. 59-1 or on the factual

 premises the interrogatories address. Relief independently warranted on the first four objections

 should issue without awaiting resolution of every financial-conflict question. ECF No. 901 16(h).
